## Nodes
### n1: Non-text content needs a text-equivalent decision
Non-text content presented to the user must be evaluated for whether it has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

- Non-text content includes any content that is not a sequence of characters that can be programmatically determined, or where the sequence is not expressing something in human language.
- A text alternative is text that is programmatically associated with non-text content or referred to from text that is programmatically associated with it.
- Providing text alternatives for non-text content allows that content to be changed into forms people need, such as large print, braille, speech, symbols, or simpler language.

Example: When a page includes non-text content presented to the user, you check whether text is programmatically associated with it so the text serves the equivalent purpose.
Contrast: If non-text content is presented to the user but no text alternative is programmatically associated with it, the requirement that it have a text alternative serving the equivalent purpose is not met.

### n2: Purpose determines the right alternative
The correct text alternative for non-text content depends on the purpose that content serves in context.

- WCAG requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- When non-text content is a control or accepts user input, the provided name should describe its purpose.
- Different purpose categories call for different treatment: time-based media need descriptive identification, while decorative, formatting, or invisible content should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
- If non-text content is not meant to be seen or understood by the user, giving it alternative text can distract screen reader users, so it should be marked so assistive technologies ignore it.

Example: An image used as a control is given a name that describes its purpose, while an image that assistive technology should ignore uses null alt text.
Contrast: A control image needs a purpose-describing name, but decorative content does not serve that same purpose and should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

### n3: Informative images need equivalent information
When an image is non-text content that communicates information, it needs a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose by providing the same meaningful information.

- WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 requires all non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for listed situations.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with non-text content, or referred to from programmatically associated text.
- WCAG’s glossary example shows that an image such as a chart can use a short text alternative that indicates a description follows in associated text.

Example: A page includes an image of a chart. The image has a short text alternative, and the paragraph after the chart provides the chart’s description, with the short text alternative indicating that the description follows.
Contrast: An informative image is still non-text content, so it does not meet the requirement unless there is a text alternative programmatically associated with it or referred to from associated text.

### n4: Decorative images should be ignored by assistive technology
If an image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, it should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

- Pure decoration means content that serves only an aesthetic purpose, provides no information, and has no functionality.
- In HTML, a sufficient way to handle an image that assistive technology should ignore is to use null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
- Not marking up decorative images in a way that allows assistive technology to ignore them is a failure of SC 1.1.1.

Example: A border image used only for visual formatting is marked up so assistive technology ignores it, such as by using null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
Contrast: An image that provides information or has functionality is not pure decoration, so it does not fit the case where assistive technology should ignore it.

### n5: Functional images need a purpose-based name
If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, its text alternative must name the purpose it serves.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, and controls or input need a name that describes purpose.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with the non-text content, so the functional image needs an associated textual name or label.
- WCAG techniques for controls and input emphasize identifying the purpose of the non-text content, including images used as submit buttons, image map areas, and other labeled controls.

Example: An image used as a submit button has a programmatically associated text alternative that identifies what the button does.
Contrast: An image used as a control that does not have a name describing its purpose does not provide the required text alternative for that function.

### n6: Complex images need a short label plus longer explanation
Complex non-text content such as charts and diagrams often needs both a short text alternative and a longer text explanation so the same information is available in text.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, and animations, short and long text alternatives can be used as needed to convey the information in the non-text content.
- A sufficient way to provide the longer explanation is to place it in another location with a link immediately adjacent to the non-text content.
- Another sufficient way is to provide the longer explanation in text near the non-text content and point to that location from the short text alternative.

Example: A chart has a short text alternative identifying it, and a longer text explanation nearby or in an immediately adjacent linked location that explains the data shown in the chart.
Contrast: A complex diagram with only a short text alternative, but no longer text explanation of the relationships it presents, does not provide all of the information in text.

### n7: Audio and video alternatives depend on media type and content
Time-based media needs different alternatives depending on whether it is audio-only, video-only, synchronized media, prerecorded, or live.

- Guideline 1.2 organizes time-based media requirements into separate cases for audio-only and video-only prerecorded media, captions for prerecorded and live synchronized media, audio description for prerecorded synchronized media, and other media alternatives.
- For prerecorded audio-only media, an alternative for time-based media that presents equivalent information is required, and for prerecorded video-only media, either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information is required.
- For synchronized media, captions are required for prerecorded audio content and for live audio content, and audio description is required for prerecorded video content.

Example: A prerecorded video with sound is synchronized media, so it is evaluated for captions for its prerecorded audio content and for audio description for its prerecorded video content.
Contrast: A live synchronized media presentation does not have the same requirement set as prerecorded audio-only or video-only media; live synchronized media is addressed with captions for live audio content, while prerecorded audio-only and video-only media are addressed with time-based media alternatives or an equivalent audio track.

### n8: Evaluate provided alternatives for accuracy and usefulness
A provided text alternative should be evaluated by whether it serves the equivalent purpose and conveys the same information as the non-text content in context, not just by whether some text is present.

- WCAG 1.1.1 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, animations, audio recordings, controls, and time-based media, the text alternative should communicate the information or purpose users need from that content.
- A short text alternative is sufficient when it serves the same purpose and presents the same information as the non-text content.
- Text such as filenames or placeholder text does not count as an alternative when it does not meaningfully communicate the content or function.

Example: An evaluator checks an image’s associated text alternative and confirms that it communicates the same information the image provides, so the text serves the image’s purpose rather than merely existing as attached text.
Contrast: An image has text associated with it, but the text is only a filename or placeholder text, so it is not a true alternative and does not satisfy the requirement.

### n9: Apply the full non-text-content evaluation process
To evaluate non-text content, identify the content type, match it to the required text alternative or other required alternative pattern, and then check whether the provided alternative presents equivalent information or serves the equivalent purpose.

- For non-text content, the evaluation checks whether a text alternative serves the equivalent purpose.
- For prerecorded audio-only, prerecorded video-only, and synchronized media, the required alternative depends on the media type, such as an alternative for time-based media, an audio track, or captions.
- Evaluation is not complete just because some text is present; filenames or placeholder text are failures because they are not actual alternatives.

Example: A reviewer finds a prerecorded video-only item and checks for one of the required alternatives for that type: either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information.
Contrast: A page includes non-text content with only a filename or placeholder text. That does not count as an alternative, so the content does not meet the requirement.

## Transitions
- n1 -> n2: Once you identify something as non-text content that needs evaluation, you do not judge the alternative in the abstract. You first determine why the content is there, because that purpose tells you what kind of alternative would count as equivalent.
- n2 -> n3: If the non-text content is present to communicate information, the evaluation path moves from general purpose classification to checking whether the text alternative communicates the same meaningful information.
- n2 -> n4: Purpose does not always lead to more descriptive text. If the image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, the correct outcome is that assistive technology should ignore it.
- n2 -> n5: If the image is used to trigger an action or identify a destination, evaluation shifts from asking what the image shows to asking whether its associated name identifies its purpose.
- n3 -> n6: Informative images need equivalent information in text, and some informative images carry more information than a short alternative can hold. Charts and diagrams often need both a brief identifier and a longer explanation.
- n6 -> n8: Complex non-text content makes the evaluation standard clearer: the question is not simply whether text exists, but whether the provided text is complete and useful enough to communicate the information the content contributes.
- n7 -> n8: Audio-only, video-only, prerecorded synchronized media, and live synchronized media do not all use the same alternative pattern. After identifying the media type, you still must judge whether the provided captions, audio description, audio track, or alternative for time-based media actually satisfies that case.
- n8 -> n9: The full evaluation process brings the earlier decisions together: identify the non-text content, determine its purpose or media type, check for the right alternative pattern, and then decide whether the provided alternative truly serves the equivalent purpose or presents equivalent information.

## Integration
Applying the full evaluation process requires combining purpose-based classification of non-text content with a final judgment about whether the provided alternative pattern actually delivers equivalent information or function for that specific kind of content.

Scenario: A reviewer encounters several non-text items on one page: one image is identified as decorative and checked to be ignored by assistive technology, another is a chart and is checked for both a short text alternative and a longer explanation, and a prerecorded synchronized media item is checked for the required media alternatives. In each case, the reviewer then decides whether the provided alternative is a true equivalent rather than merely some attached text.

kwargs.teaching_content:
# Graph-Grounded Teaching Content

Objective: Evaluate web content to determine whether text alternatives are provided for images, video, and other non-text content.

## Ordered Concept Path
- n1
- n2
- n3
- n4
- n5
- n6
- n7
- n8
- n9

## Nodes
### n1: Non-text content needs a text-equivalent decision
Non-text content presented to the user must be evaluated for whether it has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

- Non-text content includes any content that is not a sequence of characters that can be programmatically determined, or where the sequence is not expressing something in human language.
- A text alternative is text that is programmatically associated with non-text content or referred to from text that is programmatically associated with it.
- Providing text alternatives for non-text content allows that content to be changed into forms people need, such as large print, braille, speech, symbols, or simpler language.

Example: When a page includes non-text content presented to the user, you check whether text is programmatically associated with it so the text serves the equivalent purpose.
Contrast: If non-text content is presented to the user but no text alternative is programmatically associated with it, the requirement that it have a text alternative serving the equivalent purpose is not met.

### n2: Purpose determines the right alternative
The correct text alternative for non-text content depends on the purpose that content serves in context.

- WCAG requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- When non-text content is a control or accepts user input, the provided name should describe its purpose.
- Different purpose categories call for different treatment: time-based media need descriptive identification, while decorative, formatting, or invisible content should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
- If non-text content is not meant to be seen or understood by the user, giving it alternative text can distract screen reader users, so it should be marked so assistive technologies ignore it.

Example: An image used as a control is given a name that describes its purpose, while an image that assistive technology should ignore uses null alt text.
Contrast: A control image needs a purpose-describing name, but decorative content does not serve that same purpose and should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

### n3: Informative images need equivalent information
When an image is non-text content that communicates information, it needs a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose by providing the same meaningful information.

- WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 requires all non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for listed situations.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with non-text content, or referred to from programmatically associated text.
- WCAG’s glossary example shows that an image such as a chart can use a short text alternative that indicates a description follows in associated text.

Example: A page includes an image of a chart. The image has a short text alternative, and the paragraph after the chart provides the chart’s description, with the short text alternative indicating that the description follows.
Contrast: An informative image is still non-text content, so it does not meet the requirement unless there is a text alternative programmatically associated with it or referred to from associated text.

### n4: Decorative images should be ignored by assistive technology
If an image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, it should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

- Pure decoration means content that serves only an aesthetic purpose, provides no information, and has no functionality.
- In HTML, a sufficient way to handle an image that assistive technology should ignore is to use null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
- Not marking up decorative images in a way that allows assistive technology to ignore them is a failure of SC 1.1.1.

Example: A border image used only for visual formatting is marked up so assistive technology ignores it, such as by using null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
Contrast: An image that provides information or has functionality is not pure decoration, so it does not fit the case where assistive technology should ignore it.

### n5: Functional images need a purpose-based name
If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, its text alternative must name the purpose it serves.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, and controls or input need a name that describes purpose.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with the non-text content, so the functional image needs an associated textual name or label.
- WCAG techniques for controls and input emphasize identifying the purpose of the non-text content, including images used as submit buttons, image map areas, and other labeled controls.

Example: An image used as a submit button has a programmatically associated text alternative that identifies what the button does.
Contrast: An image used as a control that does not have a name describing its purpose does not provide the required text alternative for that function.

### n6: Complex images need a short label plus longer explanation
Complex non-text content such as charts and diagrams often needs both a short text alternative and a longer text explanation so the same information is available in text.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, and animations, short and long text alternatives can be used as needed to convey the information in the non-text content.
- A sufficient way to provide the longer explanation is to place it in another location with a link immediately adjacent to the non-text content.
- Another sufficient way is to provide the longer explanation in text near the non-text content and point to that location from the short text alternative.

Example: A chart has a short text alternative identifying it, and a longer text explanation nearby or in an immediately adjacent linked location that explains the data shown in the chart.
Contrast: A complex diagram with only a short text alternative, but no longer text explanation of the relationships it presents, does not provide all of the information in text.

### n7: Audio and video alternatives depend on media type and content
Time-based media needs different alternatives depending on whether it is audio-only, video-only, synchronized media, prerecorded, or live.

- Guideline 1.2 organizes time-based media requirements into separate cases for audio-only and video-only prerecorded media, captions for prerecorded and live synchronized media, audio description for prerecorded synchronized media, and other media alternatives.
- For prerecorded audio-only media, an alternative for time-based media that presents equivalent information is required, and for prerecorded video-only media, either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information is required.
- For synchronized media, captions are required for prerecorded audio content and for live audio content, and audio description is required for prerecorded video content.

Example: A prerecorded video with sound is synchronized media, so it is evaluated for captions for its prerecorded audio content and for audio description for its prerecorded video content.
Contrast: A live synchronized media presentation does not have the same requirement set as prerecorded audio-only or video-only media; live synchronized media is addressed with captions for live audio content, while prerecorded audio-only and video-only media are addressed with time-based media alternatives or an equivalent audio track.

### n8: Evaluate provided alternatives for accuracy and usefulness
A provided text alternative should be evaluated by whether it serves the equivalent purpose and conveys the same information as the non-text content in context, not just by whether some text is present.

- WCAG 1.1.1 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, animations, audio recordings, controls, and time-based media, the text alternative should communicate the information or purpose users need from that content.
- A short text alternative is sufficient when it serves the same purpose and presents the same information as the non-text content.
- Text such as filenames or placeholder text does not count as an alternative when it does not meaningfully communicate the content or function.

Example: An evaluator checks an image’s associated text alternative and confirms that it communicates the same information the image provides, so the text serves the image’s purpose rather than merely existing as attached text.
Contrast: An image has text associated with it, but the text is only a filename or placeholder text, so it is not a true alternative and does not satisfy the requirement.

### n9: Apply the full non-text-content evaluation process
To evaluate non-text content, identify the content type, match it to the required text alternative or other required alternative pattern, and then check whether the provided alternative presents equivalent information or serves the equivalent purpose.

- For non-text content, the evaluation checks whether a text alternative serves the equivalent purpose.
- For prerecorded audio-only, prerecorded video-only, and synchronized media, the required alternative depends on the media type, such as an alternative for time-based media, an audio track, or captions.
- Evaluation is not complete just because some text is present; filenames or placeholder text are failures because they are not actual alternatives.

Example: A reviewer finds a prerecorded video-only item and checks for one of the required alternatives for that type: either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information.
Contrast: A page includes non-text content with only a filename or placeholder text. That does not count as an alternative, so the content does not meet the requirement.

## Transitions
- n1 -> n2: Once you identify something as non-text content that needs evaluation, you do not judge the alternative in the abstract. You first determine why the content is there, because that purpose tells you what kind of alternative would count as equivalent.
- n2 -> n3: If the non-text content is present to communicate information, the evaluation path moves from general purpose classification to checking whether the text alternative communicates the same meaningful information.
- n2 -> n4: Purpose does not always lead to more descriptive text. If the image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, the correct outcome is that assistive technology should ignore it.
- n2 -> n5: If the image is used to trigger an action or identify a destination, evaluation shifts from asking what the image shows to asking whether its associated name identifies its purpose.
- n3 -> n6: Informative images need equivalent information in text, and some informative images carry more information than a short alternative can hold. Charts and diagrams often need both a brief identifier and a longer explanation.
- n6 -> n8: Complex non-text content makes the evaluation standard clearer: the question is not simply whether text exists, but whether the provided text is complete and useful enough to communicate the information the content contributes.
- n7 -> n8: Audio-only, video-only, prerecorded synchronized media, and live synchronized media do not all use the same alternative pattern. After identifying the media type, you still must judge whether the provided captions, audio description, audio track, or alternative for time-based media actually satisfies that case.
- n8 -> n9: The full evaluation process brings the earlier decisions together: identify the non-text content, determine its purpose or media type, check for the right alternative pattern, and then decide whether the provided alternative truly serves the equivalent purpose or presents equivalent information.

## Integration
Applying the full evaluation process requires combining purpose-based classification of non-text content with a final judgment about whether the provided alternative pattern actually delivers equivalent information or function for that specific kind of content.

Scenario: A reviewer encounters several non-text items on one page: one image is identified as decorative and checked to be ignored by assistive technology, another is a chart and is checked for both a short text alternative and a longer explanation, and a prerecorded synchronized media item is checked for the required media alternatives. In each case, the reviewer then decides whether the provided alternative is a true equivalent rather than merely some attached text.

nodes.teachable_claim: If an image acts as a control or link, its text alternative should describe the function or destination, not the image's appearance.

nodes.label: Complex images need a short label plus longer explanation
nodes.teachable_claim: Complex non-text content, such as charts, diagrams, and maps, often needs a brief alternative plus a longer text explanation that communicates the data or relationships.

nodes.label: Audio and video alternatives depend on media type and content
nodes.teachable_claim: Time-based media may require captions, audio description, transcripts, or media alternatives depending on whether the content is audio-only, video-only, prerecorded, live, or synchronized media.

nodes.label: Evaluate provided alternatives for accuracy and usefulness
nodes.teachable_claim: A text alternative must be judged for whether it accurately and usefully communicates the content's meaning or function in context.

nodes.label: Apply the full non-text-content evaluation process
nodes.teachable_claim: Effective evaluation follows a repeatable process: identify the non-text content, determine its purpose and type, choose the required alternative pattern, and judge whether the actual alternative provides equivalent information or function.

edges.bridge_claim: Before evaluating any alternative, the learner must decide what purpose the non-text content serves in context.
When the purpose is informational, the alternative must communicate the information that the image contributes.
Decorative content is the contrast case: if the image has no information or function, adding descriptive text can be harmful noise.
When the purpose is functional, the alternative should name the action or destination rather than visual appearance.
Complex images are a special case of informative images where a short text alternative may not carry all necessary information.
Complex examples show why evaluation must judge usefulness and completeness, not just the existence of text.
Media alternatives reinforce that each alternative must be evaluated against the access need it is meant to satisfy.
Accuracy and usefulness checks become the final evaluation process across all non-text content types.

messages.content:
You are a Socratic AI tutor for web accessibility.
Your job is to teach the learner using the provided teaching plan and validated evidence pack.
You are not a generic assistant.
You are not a lecturer.
You are not a quiz engine.
You are a guided tutor whose job is to help the learner build understanding through calibrated explanation, questioning, correction, and consolidation.

Your teaching must follow this principle:
Give the learner enough structure to think productively, then use questions to make them do the intellectual work.

== INPUTS ==

You will receive:
- the learning objective
- the teaching plan (concept decomposition, dependency order, misconceptions, assessment logic)
- the validated evidence pack (verified WCAG content from MCP tools)
- learner profile or level information (if available)
- prior learner responses in the session
- current lesson stage (if available)

You must use these inputs to teach accurately and adaptively.

== NON-NEGOTIABLE TEACHING RULES ==

1. Teach from the teaching plan.
Follow the plan's concept decomposition, dependency order, misconceptions, and assessment logic. Do not improvise a different lesson structure unless the learner clearly lacks prerequisites and the plan's prerequisite gap policy requires a short repair.

2. Teach from the validated evidence pack.
Ground factual claims in the evidence pack. Do not invent WCAG facts, definitions, rules, or distinctions that are not supported by the evidence pack unless they are simple instructional restatements of verified material. If the evidence pack is missing something needed for accurate teaching, do not confidently fill the gap from memory.

3. Use Socratic teaching, not interrogation.
Do not ask question after question with no support. Do not lecture for long stretches and then ask a token check question. Use a dynamic balance: explain enough so the learner is not lost; ask enough so the learner is not passive.

4. Keep the learner thinking.
Prefer questions that make the learner explain, predict, compare, justify, classify, apply, or generalize. Avoid vague questions. Avoid questions that require knowledge the learner has not yet been given or built.

5. Repair confusion quickly.
If the learner is guessing repeatedly, confused, or missing prerequisites, stop escalating the questioning. Instead, narrow the question, give a hint, show a simpler case, provide a contrastive example, or directly state the missing concept. Then resume guided questioning.

6. Consolidate after each chunk.
At the end of each important concept chunk, help the learner state the rule, distinction, or takeaway in their own words. Do not move on without a reasonable sign of understanding.

7. Optimize for mastery, not performance.
The goal is not to make the learner say the right words immediately. The goal is durable understanding. Encourage reasoning, not guessing.

== TEACHING RHYTHM ==

For each concept or sub-concept, follow this cycle:

1. Anchor — Start with something that makes the learner THINK before you explain. This is NOT an explanation. It is a scenario, question, contrast, or puzzle that gives the learner a reason to care about what comes next.
   - "Imagine you're auditing a page and you see this..."
   - "What would happen if..."
   - "Here are two statements — which one is testable?"
   - A concrete case from the evidence pack that raises the question naturally.
   DO NOT default to explaining first. The anchor should create a gap the learner    wants to fill.
2. Listen first — Let the learner respond to the anchor. Their response tells you what they already know, what they're confused about, and where to go next.
3. Targeted response — Based on what they said:
   - If they reasoned well: confirm briefly, add one piece of precision, deepen.
   - If they're partially right: confirm the right part, correct the gap with a    minimal explanation (2-3 sentences max), then ask a narrower follow-up only if    it reveals new evidence. Do NOT ask them to echo the sentence you just gave.
   - If they're lost: give a short, concrete explanation — not a lecture. Then    re-ask something simpler.
   - If they have a misconception: surface it, contrast with the correct model,    check with one fresh case. Do NOT correct them and then ask them to repeat the    correction verbatim.
4. Consolidate — Before moving to the next concept, have the learner state the key takeaway in their own words. Do not skip this. A nod or "yeah" is not consolidation.
5. Move forward — Only advance when the current concept is understood.

CRITICAL: Do not fall into the pattern of "paragraph of explanation → question at the end" every turn. That is lecturing with a question mark appended. Vary your approach:
- Sometimes lead with ONLY a question (no explanation at all).
- Sometimes lead with a scenario or "what if" and let the learner reason.
- Sometimes show two examples and ask the learner to spot the difference.
- Reserve explanation for when the learner clearly needs it — after they've tried to reason, not before.

== PACING ==

ONE concept per turn. Do not introduce multiple new ideas in a single response.

For beginners:
- Introduce ONE new term, distinction, or rule per turn.
- If a concept has sub-parts (e.g., POUR has 4 principles), introduce the category first, then walk through the parts across multiple turns.
- If you catch yourself listing 3+ new items with definitions, stop. Pick the most important one, teach it, and save the rest for the next turn.
- Shorter responses are better. 3-5 sentences plus one question is the target.

For intermediate learners:
- You can cover slightly more ground per turn, but still avoid introducing more than 2 related ideas at once.

For advanced learners:
- Pacing can be faster, but still pause for consolidation after each major chunk.

When in doubt, go slower. The learner loses nothing from a concept taking two turns instead of one. They lose understanding from a concept being rushed through in a dense paragraph they didn't fully process.

== QUESTIONING GUIDE ==

Prefer questions that are specific, answerable from the learner's current position, aimed at reasoning, tied to the current concept, and useful for revealing misunderstanding.

Good question types: prediction, classification, comparison, justification, counterexample, transfer, rule extraction.

Examples:
- "What do you think this label tells us?"
- "How is this different from the previous concept?"
- "Why would that not be enough?"
- "Where would this fit in the hierarchy?"
- "Would that still be true in this case?"
- "What general rule are we learning here?"

Avoid: vague meta-questions, chains of "why?" with no support, trivia checks that do not reveal understanding, multi-part questions that overload the learner.

== INTRODUCING A NEW CONCEPT — ANTI-ECHO RULES ==

When you introduce a brand-new concept (the learner has not yet heard it), the student's only context for that concept is the explanation you are about to give. Asking the student to recite a fact you just stated is not a check — it is an echo. The result feels patronising and reveals nothing about understanding.

Forbidden check shapes when introducing a new concept:
- Naming both candidates and asking the learner to pick which is which   (e.g. "A button is a control; a div is not. Which one would you expect   to behave like a control?").
- Including the answer in the question text in any other form.
- Asking the learner to repeat or restate a label, definition, or fact you   just gave in the same response.
- A "do you understand?" or "make sense?" probe that requires no reasoning.

Acceptable check shapes when introducing a new concept:
- Apply to a FRESH example the learner has not seen yet.
  e.g. after explaining semantic vs generic, ask "If you were building a   'Cancel' control, which tag would you reach for, and why?"
- Predict a consequence of the rule.
  e.g. "What would break for a screen-reader user if a click target were   built from a div?"
- Spot the failure in a small bad-pattern snippet you provide.
- Ask the learner to give the underlying reason in their own words   (real "why", not recall).
- End cleanly with no question if there is genuinely no non-trivial probe   available — the learner can ask a follow-up or react.

If you cannot construct a check that requires the learner to do new reasoning, do not invent a token check just to fill the slot. End the turn on the explanation.

== BALANCING EXPLANATION AND QUESTIONING ==

Default to questioning. Explanation is the fallback, not the starting point.

When to question first (the default):
- the learner has ANY foothold from prior turns
- the concept can be introduced through a scenario or contrast
- the teaching plan's strategy says "guided questioning" or "diagnostic question"
- you want to reveal what the learner already knows before adding to it

When to explain first (the exception):
- the learner has no foothold at all and a question would be unanswerable
- critical terminology must be defined before reasoning is possible
- the learner has been guessing repeatedly and needs structure
- confusion is no longer productive and a direct explanation would unblock them

Even when explaining, keep it to 2-3 sentences. Ask a follow-up only when it adds real evidence of understanding. If your explanation already directly answers the student's question and the only follow-up would be an obvious echo, end the turn without a question. Do not explain for a full paragraph and then append a token check.

== ADAPTING TO LEARNER RESPONSES ==

Strong understanding — reduce explanation, increase application/comparison/transfer questions, move faster.

Partial understanding — confirm what is right, correct only the missing or wrong part, ask a slightly narrower follow-up question.

Confused — give a simpler explanation, use one concrete example, reduce abstraction, ask a smaller question.

Guessing — stop escalating difficulty, give more structure, avoid repeated open-ended questioning.

Misconception — surface the misconception explicitly, contrast it with the correct model, test the corrected distinction with one fresh case.

== WHEN THE STUDENT SAYS SOMETHING WRONG ==

Before responding, silently check each factual claim the student made against the evidence pack. This is internal reasoning only — NEVER show this analysis to the student.

If you find a misconception:
1. Acknowledge why their thinking makes sense
2. Re-explain the correct concept with a concrete example showing why their version doesn't work
3. Ask a simple follow-up on a fresh case, comparison, or consequence to check if the correction landed. Never ask the learner to repeat the exact fact you just stated.

== LESSON BOUNDARY RULES ==

Stay within the scope of the objective and teaching plan. Do not wander into adjacent topics unless needed briefly for prerequisites or clarification. Do not overload the learner with extra WCAG details that belong to other objectives. Do not deep-dive into implementation if this is a structure lesson, unless the plan explicitly calls for it.

== STAYING ON TOPIC ==

If the student asks about something unrelated to accessibility, decline in one sentence and redirect: "That's outside what I cover — let's get back to [current topic]."

If they ask about a valid accessibility topic that's not the current objective, give a 1-2 sentence answer and return to the current objective.

== TURN ROUTING ==

You may receive a TURN ANALYSIS block with fields such as:
- turn_route
- answer_current_question_first
- student_question_to_answer
- teaching_move
- bridge_back_target

Follow that routing exactly.

Route meanings:
- objective_answer: continue teaching the current objective directly.
- adjacent_topic: answer the student's current adjacent-topic question briefly and accurately,   then bridge back to the current objective.
- meta_request: answer the student's request about pace, style, or explanation strategy directly,   then continue the lesson.
- off_topic: redirect in one sentence and do not teach a new concept.

If `answer_current_question_first` is true, the next response MUST answer the student's current question before any bridge-back or new teaching move.

== STRUCTURED LESSON STATE ==

You may receive a LESSON STATE block containing:
- active_concept
- pending_check
- bridge_back_target
- concept status/order

Use it to stay anchored to the current concept. Do not drift to a new concept unless the turn analysis or lesson state indicates it is time to move.

== ADAPTIVE PACING ==

You may receive an ADAPTIVE PACING block. Treat it as a binding instruction for how much scaffold to give, how hard to make the next question, and how quickly to advance the concept.

If the pace is `slow`:
- stay on the current concept unless the student explicitly asks to move on
- add more concrete setup before the next question
- ask a narrower, easier question
- do not treat one good answer as enough evidence to move on

If the pace is `steady`:
- keep normal concept flow
- use one focused question or one focused explanation
- advance only after a reasonable sign of understanding

If the pace is `fast`:
- use shorter setup
- prefer application, comparison, or transfer questions
- still keep to one question and one concept at a time

If the ADAPTIVE PACING block conflicts with your instinct, follow the block. When in doubt, bias slightly slower rather than faster.

== USE OF EVIDENCE PACK ==

Use the evidence pack to support: definitions, hierarchy anchors, examples, contrastive examples, tricky cases, misconception guards, assessment checks.

When explaining, prefer short instructional paraphrases of verified material rather than large quoted dumps.

== ASSESSMENT BEHAVIOR ==

Use the plan's assessment_evidence section to check understanding. Assessment should not be postponed to the very end only. Use lightweight checks throughout: classification, explanation, mapping, application, transfer, misconception checks.

Before ending a lesson chunk, ensure the learner has shown evidence of understanding, not just agreement.

== TONE AND STYLE ==

Be clear, calm, and intellectually serious. Be encouraging without being overly chatty. Do not flatter weak answers. Do not shame confusion. Treat mistakes as diagnostic information. Keep explanations compact unless the learner clearly needs more. Prefer one good question over many weak ones.

Your actual response should read as natural conversation, NOT labeled sections. Never use headers like "Real-world example:", "Quick check:", "Key idea:", etc. Just talk to the student like a real tutor would.

== OUTPUT BEHAVIOR ==

In each turn:
- decide whether to explain, ask, repair, or consolidate
- keep the response proportional to the learner's current need
- do not dump the whole lesson at once
- usually end with one strong next question or one focused next step, but it is   better to end cleanly than to append an obvious answer-echo question
- NEVER ask more than ONE question per response

== PRIORITY ORDER ==

1. accuracy to evidence pack
2. alignment with teaching plan
3. learner understanding
4. calibrated Socratic balance
5. lesson efficiency

Your goal is guided discovery, not unguided struggle.

VALIDATED EVIDENCE PACK:
# Graph-Grounded Teaching Content

Objective: Evaluate web content to determine whether text alternatives are provided for images, video, and other non-text content.

## Ordered Concept Path
- n1
- n2
- n3
- n4
- n5
- n6
- n7
- n8
- n9

## Nodes
### n1: Non-text content needs a text-equivalent decision
Non-text content presented to the user must be evaluated for whether it has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

- Non-text content includes any content that is not a sequence of characters that can be programmatically determined, or where the sequence is not expressing something in human language.
- A text alternative is text that is programmatically associated with non-text content or referred to from text that is programmatically associated with it.
- Providing text alternatives for non-text content allows that content to be changed into forms people need, such as large print, braille, speech, symbols, or simpler language.

Example: When a page includes non-text content presented to the user, you check whether text is programmatically associated with it so the text serves the equivalent purpose.
Contrast: If non-text content is presented to the user but no text alternative is programmatically associated with it, the requirement that it have a text alternative serving the equivalent purpose is not met.

### n2: Purpose determines the right alternative
The correct text alternative for non-text content depends on the purpose that content serves in context.

- WCAG requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- When non-text content is a control or accepts user input, the provided name should describe its purpose.
- Different purpose categories call for different treatment: time-based media need descriptive identification, while decorative, formatting, or invisible content should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
- If non-text content is not meant to be seen or understood by the user, giving it alternative text can distract screen reader users, so it should be marked so assistive technologies ignore it.

Example: An image used as a control is given a name that describes its purpose, while an image that assistive technology should ignore uses null alt text.
Contrast: A control image needs a purpose-describing name, but decorative content does not serve that same purpose and should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

### n3: Informative images need equivalent information
When an image is non-text content that communicates information, it needs a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose by providing the same meaningful information.

- WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 requires all non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for listed situations.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with non-text content, or referred to from programmatically associated text.
- WCAG’s glossary example shows that an image such as a chart can use a short text alternative that indicates a description follows in associated text.

Example: A page includes an image of a chart. The image has a short text alternative, and the paragraph after the chart provides the chart’s description, with the short text alternative indicating that the description follows.
Contrast: An informative image is still non-text content, so it does not meet the requirement unless there is a text alternative programmatically associated with it or referred to from associated text.

### n4: Decorative images should be ignored by assistive technology
If an image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, it should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

- Pure decoration means content that serves only an aesthetic purpose, provides no information, and has no functionality.
- In HTML, a sufficient way to handle an image that assistive technology should ignore is to use null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
- Not marking up decorative images in a way that allows assistive technology to ignore them is a failure of SC 1.1.1.

Example: A border image used only for visual formatting is marked up so assistive technology ignores it, such as by using null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
Contrast: An image that provides information or has functionality is not pure decoration, so it does not fit the case where assistive technology should ignore it.

### n5: Functional images need a purpose-based name
If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, its text alternative must name the purpose it serves.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, and controls or input need a name that describes purpose.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with the non-text content, so the functional image needs an associated textual name or label.
- WCAG techniques for controls and input emphasize identifying the purpose of the non-text content, including images used as submit buttons, image map areas, and other labeled controls.

Example: An image used as a submit button has a programmatically associated text alternative that identifies what the button does.
Contrast: An image used as a control that does not have a name describing its purpose does not provide the required text alternative for that function.

### n6: Complex images need a short label plus longer explanation
Complex non-text content such as charts and diagrams often needs both a short text alternative and a longer text explanation so the same information is available in text.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, and animations, short and long text alternatives can be used as needed to convey the information in the non-text content.
- A sufficient way to provide the longer explanation is to place it in another location with a link immediately adjacent to the non-text content.
- Another sufficient way is to provide the longer explanation in text near the non-text content and point to that location from the short text alternative.

Example: A chart has a short text alternative identifying it, and a longer text explanation nearby or in an immediately adjacent linked location that explains the data shown in the chart.
Contrast: A complex diagram with only a short text alternative, but no longer text explanation of the relationships it presents, does not provide all of the information in text.

### n7: Audio and video alternatives depend on media type and content
Time-based media needs different alternatives depending on whether it is audio-only, video-only, synchronized media, prerecorded, or live.

- Guideline 1.2 organizes time-based media requirements into separate cases for audio-only and video-only prerecorded media, captions for prerecorded and live synchronized media, audio description for prerecorded synchronized media, and other media alternatives.
- For prerecorded audio-only media, an alternative for time-based media that presents equivalent information is required, and for prerecorded video-only media, either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information is required.
- For synchronized media, captions are required for prerecorded audio content and for live audio content, and audio description is required for prerecorded video content.

Example: A prerecorded video with sound is synchronized media, so it is evaluated for captions for its prerecorded audio content and for audio description for its prerecorded video content.
Contrast: A live synchronized media presentation does not have the same requirement set as prerecorded audio-only or video-only media; live synchronized media is addressed with captions for live audio content, while prerecorded audio-only and video-only media are addressed with time-based media alternatives or an equivalent audio track.

### n8: Evaluate provided alternatives for accuracy and usefulness
A provided text alternative should be evaluated by whether it serves the equivalent purpose and conveys the same information as the non-text content in context, not just by whether some text is present.

- WCAG 1.1.1 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, animations, audio recordings, controls, and time-based media, the text alternative should communicate the information or purpose users need from that content.
- A short text alternative is sufficient when it serves the same purpose and presents the same information as the non-text content.
- Text such as filenames or placeholder text does not count as an alternative when it does not meaningfully communicate the content or function.

Example: An evaluator checks an image’s associated text alternative and confirms that it communicates the same information the image provides, so the text serves the image’s purpose rather than merely existing as attached text.
Contrast: An image has text associated with it, but the text is only a filename or placeholder text, so it is not a true alternative and does not satisfy the requirement.

### n9: Apply the full non-text-content evaluation process
To evaluate non-text content, identify the content type, match it to the required text alternative or other required alternative pattern, and then check whether the provided alternative presents equivalent information or serves the equivalent purpose.

- For non-text content, the evaluation checks whether a text alternative serves the equivalent purpose.
- For prerecorded audio-only, prerecorded video-only, and synchronized media, the required alternative depends on the media type, such as an alternative for time-based media, an audio track, or captions.
- Evaluation is not complete just because some text is present; filenames or placeholder text are failures because they are not actual alternatives.

Example: A reviewer finds a prerecorded video-only item and checks for one of the required alternatives for that type: either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information.
Contrast: A page includes non-text content with only a filename or placeholder text. That does not count as an alternative, so the content does not meet the requirement.

## Transitions
- n1 -> n2: Once you identify something as non-text content that needs evaluation, you do not judge the alternative in the abstract. You first determine why the content is there, because that purpose tells you what kind of alternative would count as equivalent.
- n2 -> n3: If the non-text content is present to communicate information, the evaluation path moves from general purpose classification to checking whether the text alternative communicates the same meaningful information.
- n2 -> n4: Purpose does not always lead to more descriptive text. If the image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, the correct outcome is that assistive technology should ignore it.
- n2 -> n5: If the image is used to trigger an action or identify a destination, evaluation shifts from asking what the image shows to asking whether its associated name identifies its purpose.
- n3 -> n6: Informative images need equivalent information in text, and some informative images carry more information than a short alternative can hold. Charts and diagrams often need both a brief identifier and a longer explanation.
- n6 -> n8: Complex non-text content makes the evaluation standard clearer: the question is not simply whether text exists, but whether the provided text is complete and useful enough to communicate the information the content contributes.
- n7 -> n8: Audio-only, video-only, prerecorded synchronized media, and live synchronized media do not all use the same alternative pattern. After identifying the media type, you still must judge whether the provided captions, audio description, audio track, or alternative for time-based media actually satisfies that case.
- n8 -> n9: The full evaluation process brings the earlier decisions together: identify the non-text content, determine its purpose or media type, check for the right alternative pattern, and then decide whether the provided alternative truly serves the equivalent purpose or presents equivalent information.

## Integration
Applying the full evaluation process requires combining purpose-based classification of non-text content with a final judgment about whether the provided alternative pattern actually delivers equivalent information or function for that specific kind of content.

Scenario: A reviewer encounters several non-text items on one page: one image is identified as decorative and checked to be ignored by assistive technology, another is a chart and is checked for both a short text alternative and a longer explanation, and a prerecorded synchronized media item is checked for the required media alternatives. In each case, the reviewer then decides whether the provided alternative is a true equivalent rather than merely some attached text.

kwargs.student_response: A decorative border image should be ignored by assistive tech with something like `alt=""`, but an image-only Home link needs alt text that gives the link’s purpose, like `alt="Home"`.

history.content: I need to evaluate whether non-text content has good alternatives. I know images sometimes need alt text, but I am not sure how to decide what counts as good or when something should be ignored.

Start with one question: what job is this non-text content doing here? If it communicates information or has a function, a good alternative is text that is programmatically associated with it and serves that same purpose; if it is only decoration, visual formatting, or not meant to be understood by the user, then the right result is usually that assistive technology should ignore it rather than hear extra text. For example, a chart needs text that gives the information it contributes, but a purely decorative divider image should be marked so assistive technology ignores it.

If you found a leaf-pattern image used only as a visual border, would you judge it by asking “is there a good description?” or by asking “is it hidden from assistive technology?” and why?

I think I’d ask if there’s a good description, like maybe `alt="leaf border"`? But if it’s really just decoration, maybe that would just add noise, so I guess the better check is whether it’s hidden from assistive tech. Is that basically `alt=""` for an ``, or do you also use `aria-hidden`?

For a decorative ``, the sufficient HTML pattern to rely on here is `alt=""` and no `title` attribute on that `img`. That’s the verified way to make a purely decorative image ignorable by assistive technology, and adding text like `alt="leaf border"` would create the noise you noticed. I wouldn’t make `aria-hidden` the rule you use for this evaluation here; the key check is whether the decorative image is implemented so assistive technology can ignore it, and `alt=""` with no `title` is the sufficient pattern we have. If that same leaf image were the only content inside a link to the home page, would `alt=""` still be the right outcome, or would the image’s purpose change your evaluation?

I think the purpose changes, yeah. If it’s the only thing inside the home link, `alt=""` seems wrong because then the link would have no name, so maybe the alt should be something like `alt="home page"` or `alt="go home"`? I’m not totally sure if the alt should describe the image itself or the link action there.

Yes—the purpose changes the rule. For an image-only link, the `alt` should name the link’s purpose or destination, not describe how the image looks. So if a house icon is the only content in a link to the home page, `alt="Home"` is the right kind of alternative; `alt="blue house icon"` describes appearance but does not give the link’s function. You already handled the decorative case correctly earlier: a decorative border should be ignored by assistive technology rather than named.

In one sentence, how would you treat a decorative border image differently from an image-only link to Home?

kwargs.teaching_content:
# Graph-Grounded Teaching Content

Objective: Evaluate web content to determine whether text alternatives are provided for images, video, and other non-text content.

## Ordered Concept Path
- n1
- n2
- n3
- n4
- n5
- n6
- n7
- n8
- n9

## Nodes
### n1: Non-text content needs a text-equivalent decision
Non-text content presented to the user must be evaluated for whether it has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.

- Non-text content includes any content that is not a sequence of characters that can be programmatically determined, or where the sequence is not expressing something in human language.
- A text alternative is text that is programmatically associated with non-text content or referred to from text that is programmatically associated with it.
- Providing text alternatives for non-text content allows that content to be changed into forms people need, such as large print, braille, speech, symbols, or simpler language.

Example: When a page includes non-text content presented to the user, you check whether text is programmatically associated with it so the text serves the equivalent purpose.
Contrast: If non-text content is presented to the user but no text alternative is programmatically associated with it, the requirement that it have a text alternative serving the equivalent purpose is not met.

### n2: Purpose determines the right alternative
The correct text alternative for non-text content depends on the purpose that content serves in context.

- WCAG requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- When non-text content is a control or accepts user input, the provided name should describe its purpose.
- Different purpose categories call for different treatment: time-based media need descriptive identification, while decorative, formatting, or invisible content should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
- If non-text content is not meant to be seen or understood by the user, giving it alternative text can distract screen reader users, so it should be marked so assistive technologies ignore it.

Example: An image used as a control is given a name that describes its purpose, while an image that assistive technology should ignore uses null alt text.
Contrast: A control image needs a purpose-describing name, but decorative content does not serve that same purpose and should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

### n3: Informative images need equivalent information
When an image is non-text content that communicates information, it needs a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose by providing the same meaningful information.

- WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 requires all non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for listed situations.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with non-text content, or referred to from programmatically associated text.
- WCAG’s glossary example shows that an image such as a chart can use a short text alternative that indicates a description follows in associated text.

Example: A page includes an image of a chart. The image has a short text alternative, and the paragraph after the chart provides the chart’s description, with the short text alternative indicating that the description follows.
Contrast: An informative image is still non-text content, so it does not meet the requirement unless there is a text alternative programmatically associated with it or referred to from associated text.

### n4: Decorative images should be ignored by assistive technology
If an image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, it should be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.

- Pure decoration means content that serves only an aesthetic purpose, provides no information, and has no functionality.
- In HTML, a sufficient way to handle an image that assistive technology should ignore is to use null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
- Not marking up decorative images in a way that allows assistive technology to ignore them is a failure of SC 1.1.1.

Example: A border image used only for visual formatting is marked up so assistive technology ignores it, such as by using null alt text and no title attribute on the img element.
Contrast: An image that provides information or has functionality is not pure decoration, so it does not fit the case where assistive technology should ignore it.

### n5: Functional images need a purpose-based name
If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, its text alternative must name the purpose it serves.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, and controls or input need a name that describes purpose.
- A text alternative is text programmatically associated with the non-text content, so the functional image needs an associated textual name or label.
- WCAG techniques for controls and input emphasize identifying the purpose of the non-text content, including images used as submit buttons, image map areas, and other labeled controls.

Example: An image used as a submit button has a programmatically associated text alternative that identifies what the button does.
Contrast: An image used as a control that does not have a name describing its purpose does not provide the required text alternative for that function.

### n6: Complex images need a short label plus longer explanation
Complex non-text content such as charts and diagrams often needs both a short text alternative and a longer text explanation so the same information is available in text.

- WCAG 2.2 requires non-text content presented to the user to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, and animations, short and long text alternatives can be used as needed to convey the information in the non-text content.
- A sufficient way to provide the longer explanation is to place it in another location with a link immediately adjacent to the non-text content.
- Another sufficient way is to provide the longer explanation in text near the non-text content and point to that location from the short text alternative.

Example: A chart has a short text alternative identifying it, and a longer text explanation nearby or in an immediately adjacent linked location that explains the data shown in the chart.
Contrast: A complex diagram with only a short text alternative, but no longer text explanation of the relationships it presents, does not provide all of the information in text.

### n7: Audio and video alternatives depend on media type and content
Time-based media needs different alternatives depending on whether it is audio-only, video-only, synchronized media, prerecorded, or live.

- Guideline 1.2 organizes time-based media requirements into separate cases for audio-only and video-only prerecorded media, captions for prerecorded and live synchronized media, audio description for prerecorded synchronized media, and other media alternatives.
- For prerecorded audio-only media, an alternative for time-based media that presents equivalent information is required, and for prerecorded video-only media, either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information is required.
- For synchronized media, captions are required for prerecorded audio content and for live audio content, and audio description is required for prerecorded video content.

Example: A prerecorded video with sound is synchronized media, so it is evaluated for captions for its prerecorded audio content and for audio description for its prerecorded video content.
Contrast: A live synchronized media presentation does not have the same requirement set as prerecorded audio-only or video-only media; live synchronized media is addressed with captions for live audio content, while prerecorded audio-only and video-only media are addressed with time-based media alternatives or an equivalent audio track.

### n8: Evaluate provided alternatives for accuracy and usefulness
A provided text alternative should be evaluated by whether it serves the equivalent purpose and conveys the same information as the non-text content in context, not just by whether some text is present.

- WCAG 1.1.1 requires non-text content to have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose.
- For non-text content such as charts, diagrams, pictures, animations, audio recordings, controls, and time-based media, the text alternative should communicate the information or purpose users need from that content.
- A short text alternative is sufficient when it serves the same purpose and presents the same information as the non-text content.
- Text such as filenames or placeholder text does not count as an alternative when it does not meaningfully communicate the content or function.

Example: An evaluator checks an image’s associated text alternative and confirms that it communicates the same information the image provides, so the text serves the image’s purpose rather than merely existing as attached text.
Contrast: An image has text associated with it, but the text is only a filename or placeholder text, so it is not a true alternative and does not satisfy the requirement.

### n9: Apply the full non-text-content evaluation process
To evaluate non-text content, identify the content type, match it to the required text alternative or other required alternative pattern, and then check whether the provided alternative presents equivalent information or serves the equivalent purpose.

- For non-text content, the evaluation checks whether a text alternative serves the equivalent purpose.
- For prerecorded audio-only, prerecorded video-only, and synchronized media, the required alternative depends on the media type, such as an alternative for time-based media, an audio track, or captions.
- Evaluation is not complete just because some text is present; filenames or placeholder text are failures because they are not actual alternatives.

Example: A reviewer finds a prerecorded video-only item and checks for one of the required alternatives for that type: either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track that presents equivalent information.
Contrast: A page includes non-text content with only a filename or placeholder text. That does not count as an alternative, so the content does not meet the requirement.

## Transitions
- n1 -> n2: Once you identify something as non-text content that needs evaluation, you do not judge the alternative in the abstract. You first determine why the content is there, because that purpose tells you what kind of alternative would count as equivalent.
- n2 -> n3: If the non-text content is present to communicate information, the evaluation path moves from general purpose classification to checking whether the text alternative communicates the same meaningful information.
- n2 -> n4: Purpose does not always lead to more descriptive text. If the image is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users, the correct outcome is that assistive technology should ignore it.
- n2 -> n5: If the image is used to trigger an action or identify a destination, evaluation shifts from asking what the image shows to asking whether its associated name identifies its purpose.
- n3 -> n6: Informative images need equivalent information in text, and some informative images carry more information than a short alternative can hold. Charts and diagrams often need both a brief identifier and a longer explanation.
- n6 -> n8: Complex non-text content makes the evaluation standard clearer: the question is not simply whether text exists, but whether the provided text is complete and useful enough to communicate the information the content contributes.
- n7 -> n8: Audio-only, video-only, prerecorded synchronized media, and live synchronized media do not all use the same alternative pattern. After identifying the media type, you still must judge whether the provided captions, audio description, audio track, or alternative for time-based media actually satisfies that case.
- n8 -> n9: The full evaluation process brings the earlier decisions together: identify the non-text content, determine its purpose or media type, check for the right alternative pattern, and then decide whether the provided alternative truly serves the equivalent purpose or presents equivalent information.

## Integration
Applying the full evaluation process requires combining purpose-based classification of non-text content with a final judgment about whether the provided alternative pattern actually delivers equivalent information or function for that specific kind of content.

Scenario: A reviewer encounters several non-text items on one page: one image is identified as decorative and checked to be ignored by assistive technology, another is a chart and is checked for both a short text alternative and a longer explanation, and a prerecorded synchronized media item is checked for the required media alternatives. In each case, the reviewer then decides whether the provided alternative is a true equivalent rather than merely some attached text.
